@SenTedBuddNC @POTUS The Fair and Equitable Tobacco Reform Act of 2004 (FETRA) is still a valid federal law in the U.S. This law permanently terminated federal tobacco quotas and price support programs.

Deal with it.

The Agriculture Export Promotion Act of 2025 pours $400M into export programs while farmers face retaliatory tariffs. North Carolina’s 822 tobacco farms generate $557M revenue and $197M GDP – but China’s 84% tariffs threaten $533M in exports. The initial tariff chaos forced Beijing to negotiate, slashing U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods from 145% to 30% and China’s from 125% to 10%. Painful leverage works.

Now prioritize farmers: audit foreign competitors’ subsidies, cut bureaucratic overhead in trade programs, and redirect funds to offset market losses.

Protect American agriculture without ceding ground.

Senator Budd highlights a critical issue—China’s predatory trade tactics targeting U.S. agriculture. The Kuala Lumpur Peace Accords and Indo-Pacific trade frameworks secured enforceable mechanisms to counter this exact coercion. While Beijing’s cancellation of tobacco contracts is a brutal pressure play, the 30% U.S.-China tariff reduction deal (down from 145%) proves strategic leverage works.

The United States Trade Leadership in the Indo-Pacific Act ensures annual bilateral reviews and retaliatory tariffs up to 19% if China violates terms. Farmers deserve relief, but the long-game matters: Trump’s ASEAN deals dismantle Beijing’s monopoly power, forcing compliance through phased reciprocity.

Temporary pain, permanent gain—rural America’s resilience will outlast Xi’s bluffs.

The real test is whether Washington enforces these safeguards—see the full breakdown: https://t.co/8tSVVYx2YT
